data.scenario_text: The function <me>d(x)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)\right]+13</me> models the depth of the water, in feet, at a harbor, where <m>x</m> is the number of hours after midnight and <m>x=0</m> represents midnight.
data.part_a: What is the average depth of the water at this harbor?
data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times a day does high tide occur?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 3:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=13, so the water averages \boxed{13\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=13+4=17\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=13-4=9\text{ ft}

high tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 17\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 9\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[9\text{ ft},\ 17\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 2 hours to the right: at 2:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 5:00 a.m. and again at 5:00 p.m.; low tide is at 11:00 a.m. and again at 11:00 p.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=3 (3:00 a.m.):

d(3)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(3-2)\right]+13=4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+13=17\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{17.0\text{ ft}} at 3:00 a.m..

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the water averages \boxed{12\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ ft}

high tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 16\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 8\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[8\text{ ft},\ 16\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 3 hours to the right: at 3:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 6:00 a.m. and again at 6:00 p.m.; low tide is at noon and again at midnight.

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=13, so the water averages \boxed{13\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=13+6=19\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=13-6=7\text{ ft}

high tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 19\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 7\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[7\text{ ft},\ 19\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 3 hours to the right: at 3:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 6:00 a.m. and again at 6:00 p.m.; low tide is at noon and again at midnight.

data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times a day does high tide occur?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 10:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=14, so the water averages \boxed{14\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=14+6=20\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=14-6=8\text{ ft}

high tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 20\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 8\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[8\text{ ft},\ 20\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 2 hours to the right: at 2:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 5:00 a.m. and again at 5:00 p.m.; low tide is at 11:00 a.m. and again at 11:00 p.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (10:00 a.m.):

d(10)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-2)\right]+14=6\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+14=-3 \, \sqrt{3} + 14 \approx 8.8\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{8.8\text{ ft}} at 10:00 a.m..

\text{maximum}=15+4=19\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=15-4=11\text{ ft}

high tide is at 7:00 a.m., when the depth is 19\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 1:00 p.m., when the depth is 11\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[11\text{ ft},\ 19\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times a day does high tide occur?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at noon. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=13, so the water averages \boxed{13\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=13+4=17\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=13-4=9\text{ ft}

high tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 17\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 9\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[9\text{ ft},\ 17\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 2 hours to the right: at 2:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 5:00 a.m. and again at 5:00 p.m.; low tide is at 11:00 a.m. and again at 11:00 p.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=12 (noon):

d(12)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(12-2)\right]+13=4\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+13=-2 \, \sqrt{3} + 13 \approx 9.5\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{9.5\text{ ft}} at noon.

data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 11:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=13, so the water averages \boxed{13\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=13+6=19\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=13-6=7\text{ ft}

high tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 19\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 7\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[7\text{ ft},\ 19\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 3 hours to the right: at 3:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 6:00 a.m. and again at 6:00 p.m.; low tide is at noon and again at midnight.

Part (e). Substitute x=11 (11:00 a.m.):

d(11)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(11-3)\right]+13=6\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+13=-3 \, \sqrt{3} + 13 \approx 7.8\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{7.8\text{ ft}} at 11:00 a.m..

data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times a day does high tide occur?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at noon. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=10, so the water averages \boxed{10\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=10+6=16\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=10-6=4\text{ ft}

high tide is at 7:00 a.m., when the depth is 16\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 1:00 p.m., when the depth is 4\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[4\text{ ft},\ 16\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

The phase shift is \boxed{4} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 4 hours to the right: at 4:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 7:00 a.m. and again at 7:00 p.m.; low tide is at 1:00 p.m. and again at 1:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=12 (noon):

d(12)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(12-4)\right]+10=6\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+10=-3 \, \sqrt{3} + 10 \approx 4.8\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{4.8\text{ ft}} at noon.

data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times a day does high tide occur?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 10:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=15, so the water averages \boxed{15\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=15+6=21\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=15-6=9\text{ ft}

high tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 21\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 9\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[9\text{ ft},\ 21\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 2 hours to the right: at 2:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 5:00 a.m. and again at 5:00 p.m.; low tide is at 11:00 a.m. and again at 11:00 p.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (10:00 a.m.):

d(10)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-2)\right]+15=6\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+15=-3 \, \sqrt{3} + 15 \approx 9.8\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{9.8\text{ ft}} at 10:00 a.m..

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=10+6=16\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=10-6=4\text{ ft}

high tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 16\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 4\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[4\text{ ft},\ 16\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times a day does high tide occur?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 7:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=9, so the water averages \boxed{9\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=9+6=15\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=9-6=3\text{ ft}

high tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 15\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 3\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[3\text{ ft},\ 15\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 5 hours to the right: at 5:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 8:00 a.m. and again at 8:00 p.m.; low tide is at 2:00 p.m. and again at 2:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=7 (7:00 a.m.):

d(7)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(7-5)\right]+9=6\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+9=3 \, \sqrt{3} + 9 \approx 14.2\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{14.2\text{ ft}} at 7:00 a.m..

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the water averages \boxed{12\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ ft}

high tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 16\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 8\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[8\text{ ft},\ 16\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

\text{maximum}=15+6=21\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=15-6=9\text{ ft}

high tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 21\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 9\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[9\text{ ft},\ 21\text{ ft}]}.

data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times a day does high tide occur?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 7:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=13, so the water averages \boxed{13\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=13+4=17\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=13-4=9\text{ ft}

high tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 17\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 9\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[9\text{ ft},\ 17\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 3 hours to the right: at 3:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 6:00 a.m. and again at 6:00 p.m.; low tide is at noon and again at midnight.

Part (e). Substitute x=7 (7:00 a.m.):

d(7)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(7-3)\right]+13=4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+13=2 \, \sqrt{3} + 13 \approx 16.5\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{16.5\text{ ft}} at 7:00 a.m..

data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times a day does high tide occur?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 10:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=10, so the water averages \boxed{10\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=10+4=14\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=10-4=6\text{ ft}

high tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 14\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 6\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[6\text{ ft},\ 14\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 2 hours to the right: at 2:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 5:00 a.m. and again at 5:00 p.m.; low tide is at 11:00 a.m. and again at 11:00 p.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (10:00 a.m.):

d(10)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-2)\right]+10=4\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+10=-2 \, \sqrt{3} + 10 \approx 6.5\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{6.5\text{ ft}} at 10:00 a.m..

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=13, so the water averages \boxed{13\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=13+4=17\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=13-4=9\text{ ft}

high tide is at 7:00 a.m., when the depth is 17\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 1:00 p.m., when the depth is 9\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[9\text{ ft},\ 17\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

The phase shift is \boxed{4} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 4 hours to the right: at 4:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 7:00 a.m. and again at 7:00 p.m.; low tide is at 1:00 p.m. and again at 1:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=6 (6:00 a.m.):

d(6)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(6-4)\right]+13=4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+13=2 \, \sqrt{3} + 13 \approx 16.5\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{16.5\text{ ft}} at 6:00 a.m..

data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times a day does high tide occur?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at noon. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=13, so the water averages \boxed{13\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=13+6=19\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=13-6=7\text{ ft}

high tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 19\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 7\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[7\text{ ft},\ 19\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 2 hours to the right: at 2:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 5:00 a.m. and again at 5:00 p.m.; low tide is at 11:00 a.m. and again at 11:00 p.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=12 (noon):

d(12)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(12-2)\right]+13=6\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+13=-3 \, \sqrt{3} + 13 \approx 7.8\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{7.8\text{ ft}} at noon.
